finding_list.consequence: The UPDATE of password_hash is not awaited. The route proceeds to delete other sessions and returns { ok: true } even if the update fails or has not completed; a rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection (outside the try/catch, so it can crash the Node process by default) and the user is told the password changed while the old password remains, with other sessions already revoked.

payments.charge catches every Stripe error (declined card, network failure) and returns undefined. The route's check `payment && payment.status !== 'succeeded'` is then false, so the order is marked 'paid' with a null payment_intent_id and a 201 is returned. Customers get goods without paying.

redeem reads times_used with a plain SELECT and writes back times_used + 1 as an absolute value. Two concurrent checkouts both read the same count, both pass the max_uses check, and both write the same increment, so a limited coupon is redeemed more often than allowed (and the counter under-counts). This costs real discount money.

When Stripe throws (declined card, authentication required, network error), charge() logs and returns undefined. Checkout treats undefined as success, marks the order paid with a null payment_intent_id and returns 201, so customers get orders without paying, and those orders cannot be refunded.

The unauthenticated search endpoint concatenates q and category into the SQL string, so an attacker can inject SQL to read arbitrary tables (users, sessions, orders), bypass the active filter, or modify data depending on DB privileges.
Any signed-in customer can read any other customer's order, including shipping address and items, by guessing or enumerating order ids (IDOR).
